label: The Complex Projective Line
notes: This chapter spans printed pages 311 to 328 and builds a working model of the complex projective line. Adding one point at infinity fuses complex numbers, circles, lines, Mobius maps, inversions, cross-ratios, and a sphere into a single geometry. Stress that infinity is structural, not a distant pixel for the audience.

label: Two Charts for CP1
notes: Emphasize that a finite number is the class of the pair z comma one, while infinity is one comma zero. CP1 needs two overlapping charts, not one plane with a label glued on. The reciprocal chart sends large modulus points near the origin, placing infinity cleanly at w equals zero.

label: The Riemann Sphere
notes: Walk through stereographic projection slowly. The sphere sits tangent to the plane, projection runs from the north pole, and every finite complex number lands on the sphere. Large modulus points crowd toward the pole, so infinity becomes the north pole and completes the surface. This is the global picture of CP1.

label: Mobius Transformations
notes: Present the Mobius map as a matrix acting on homogeneous coordinates, then dehomogenized to the familiar fraction. Insist on the nondegeneracy condition a d minus b c nonzero. Grid lines bend into arcs, but the projective content is invariant: generalized circles map to generalized circles under every such map.

label: PGL(2,C)
notes: Explain why the matrix is defined only up to nonzero scale, which collapses four complex entries into three complex degrees of freedom. The projectivities of CP1 form the group PGL of two over C. Composition is matrix multiplication, so the whole symmetry group reduces to clean linear algebra.

label: The Complex Cross-Ratio
notes: Define the cross-ratio of four points as a ratio of differences and state its central property: it is invariant under every Mobius transformation. Connect this to slide five, since three degrees of freedom let us send any three points to zero, one, and infinity, after which the cross-ratio is the image of the fourth.

label: Real Cross-Ratio Detects Circles
notes: State the key theorem crisply: four points are concyclic or collinear exactly when their cross-ratio is real or infinite. Demonstrate with the imaginary part as a side predicate, which is zero on the boundary circle and opposite signs inside and outside. Cocircularity becomes a projective fact on CP1.

label: Circles and Lines Unified
notes: Bring lines and circles together as one family of generalized circles. On the sphere a line is simply a circle that passes through the north pole, while a finite circle avoids it. Mobius maps permute this single family, which is why distinguishing line from circle is no longer fundamental.

label: Inversions and Reflections
notes: Contrast Mobius and anti-Mobius maps. Conjugation is a field automorphism with no projective matrix, so it preserves the circle family but reverses oriented sidedness. Unit-circle inversion fixes the unit circle pointwise, swaps origin with infinity, and exchanges inside with outside. These are the orientation-reversing symmetries.

label: Grassmann-Plucker and Ptolemy
notes: Show the two-coordinate bracket as a complex determinant and write the rank-two Grassmann-Plucker relation. For finite points the bracket is just a difference, so the three summands are complex vectors. Taking magnitudes and applying the triangle inequality casts a Euclidean shadow that is exactly Ptolemy's inequality.

label: Intersection Angles
notes: Encode two oriented circles through their shared points using auxiliary points, then read the argument of a cross-ratio as the signed angle between their oriented tangents. Reversing either orientation flips the sign. Because Mobius maps preserve cross-ratios, they preserve this signed angle, so the geometry is conformal.

label: Recap
notes: Recap the chain of translations. Homogeneous coordinates define infinity, cross-ratios make the circle test projective and record sidedness and angle, Mobius maps preserve all of it while anti-Mobius maps flip orientation, Grassmann-Plucker yields Ptolemy, and stereographic projection reveals CP1 as a sphere for the audience.
